newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic faces uphill struggle for presidency.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic faces uphill struggle for presidency.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, running for the presidency of Yugoslavia, faces resistance to his plans to tailor the post to his needs from an unexpected quarter, diplomats said on Friday.
"He is now held hostage by Montenegrins, loath to allow changes to the federal constitution and give him the sweeping powers he craves," a senior Western diplomat said.
Serbia and its tiny ally Montenegro make up the new Yugoslavia formed after the violent break-up of the former six-member Balkan federation in 1991.
Zoran Lilic, the current Yugoslav president with largely ceremonial powers, was elected by the parliament. His term expires on June 25.

Milosevic, the real power in Yugoslavia and master of brinksmanship, is about to complete his second term as president of Serbia and cannot stand again so the only way ahead for him is to take over the Yugoslav presidency.

But to rule in the authoritarian way he was accustomed to in Serbia -- holding ultimate power over the police, army, purse and policy -- he must change the federal constitution and that can be done only in consensus with Montenegro.
"This is where the surprise and the fun starts," the diplomat said.

Diplomats believe Milosevic created the problem when he tried to oust the reformist faction in Montenegro led by Prime Minister Milo Djukanovic to pave the way for an uncontested amending of the constitution.
But his ally, Montenegro's President Momir Bulatovic, failed to oust Djukanovic, a charismatic 35-year old pro-western politician, who survived and consolidated party resistance to Belgrade.
On Thursday, Montenegro's Democratic Party of Socialists (DPS) balked at a proposal by Milosevic's Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS) to amend the federal constitution.
Despite assurances that the changes were needed only to enable Milosevic to be elected by direct and secret ballot, the DPS feared the reforms could have wider impact.
"It looks like a marginal change but it could alter Montenegro's position in the federation," DPS vice president Milica Pejanovic Djurisic said.
On Friday, Djukanovic dispelled any remaining hope that it might come round in a scathing attack openly accused Bulatovic of selling out to Milosevic.
"No-one has the right to forge secret political deals to the detriment of Montenegro, its dignity, political equality and democratic processes," Djukanovic told reporters.

"All of us are obliged to oppose such attempts within our powers and competence, because this issue is more important and older than any policy, any regime or any individual career - this is the issue of Montenegro's dignity and prospects."
Djukanovic has frequently urged Milosevic to implement the Dayton peace accords to enable sanctions barring Serbia and Montenegro from desperately need foreign funds to be lifted.

"The federation can survive only as a democratic community of equal republics and citizens, if it embarks upon deep economic reforms and full integration in the international community," he said on Friday.
"It is a standoff for the time being. Milosevic can either strike a deal with Djukanovic, which would be probably very expensive given Djukanovic's demands," the diplomat said.
"Milosevic's other option is to take the post as it is and gradually assume power, much in the same way he did as president of Serbia," he said.
